validation.note: Generated structured draft records; numeric-entry and complex-format keys require clinical/editorial completion before production exam use.

items.title: A client with a tracheostomy develops distress and no airflow through the tube. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Call for help, assess inner cannula and patency, remove/replace obstructed inner cannula per protocol, and provide oxygen to stoma/face as appropriate.
items.rationale: Mucus plugging can obstruct the artificial airway; rapid patency assessment and oxygenation are critical.

items.title: A fresh tracheostomy placed yesterday becomes dislodged. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Activate emergency airway response; do not blindly reinsert into immature tract; oxygenate and prepare expert airway management.
items.rationale: A fresh tract can create a false passage; reinsertion requires experienced personnel and emergency planning.

items.title: A young adult reports chest pain and agitation after cocaine use; BP 188/110 mm Hg. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Obtain ECG, monitor for ischemia/dysrhythmia, reduce sympathetic stimulation with prescribed benzodiazepine, and follow ACS evaluation.
items.rationale: Cocaine increases myocardial oxygen demand and vasoconstriction; benzodiazepines help control adrenergic excess.

items.title: A client has BP 224/128 mm Hg with acute confusion and retinal hemorrhages. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client has BP 224/128 mm Hg with acute confusion and retinal hemorrhages.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Activate emergency response, assess end-organ injury, establish monitoring, and administer titratable IV antihypertensive as prescribed.
items.rationale: Severe BP with acute target-organ damage is a hypertensive emergency requiring controlled reduction.

items.title: An older adult becomes dizzy when standing; BP falls from 138/78 supine to 104/62 standing. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:An older adult becomes dizzy when standing; BP falls from 138/78 supine to 104/62 standing.|response:Assist to sit/lie down, assess volume and medications, teach slow position changes, and use fall precautions.|rationale:A symptomatic orthostatic drop increases fall risk and may reflect medication or volume issues.
items.rationale: A symptomatic orthostatic drop increases fall risk and may reflect medication or volume issues.

items.title: A client briefly loses consciousness while standing and has palpitations before the event. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Syncope evaluation|priority:Assess ABCs, ECG, orthostatic vitals, glucose, and injury; escalate if cardiac symptoms or abnormal findings.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Syncope with palpitations may indicate dysrhythmia and requires cardiac evaluation.

items.title: An older adult with exertional syncope has a harsh systolic murmur radiating to the carotids. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Aortic stenosis|actions:Assess hemodynamic stability, avoid exertion, and arrange prompt cardiac evaluation; report syncope urgently.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Classic symptoms of severe aortic stenosis include angina, syncope, and dyspnea.

items.title: A client with a prosthetic valve has fever, new murmur, and positive blood cultures. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with a prosthetic valve has fever, new murmur, and positive blood cultures.|priority:Obtain ordered cultures before antibiotics when feasible, monitor embolic/heart-failure signs, and administer prolonged IV antimicrobials as prescribed.
items.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis carries high complication risk and requires organism-directed therapy.

items.title: A client has sharp chest pain relieved by leaning forward and diffuse ST elevation. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Positional pleuritic pain and diffuse ST changes suggest pericarditis; tamponade is a critical complication.

items.title: A client after myocardial infarction asks when to resume exercise. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Supervised progression improves recovery while monitoring for ischemic symptoms.

items.title: A client has calf pain with walking relieved by rest, diminished pulses, and cool feet. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Promote supervised walking, smoking cessation, foot care, and prescribed antiplatelet/statin therapy; report rest pain or tissue loss.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Intermittent claudication reflects arterial insufficiency; risk-factor management and exercise improve function.

items.title: A client has bilateral ankle edema, brown lower-leg discoloration, and shallow irregular ulcers near the medial malleoli. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Assess arterial perfusion before compression, elevate legs, support compression therapy if appropriate, and provide wound care.
items.rationale: Venous hypertension causes edema and gaiter-area ulcers; compression is used only after arterial status is assessed.

items.title: A client has arm swelling on the side of axillary node dissection. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Lymphedema after mastectomy|actions:Encourage prescribed compression/exercise and skin care, avoid trauma, and report redness/fever; follow individualized limb precautions.|evaluation:Lymphatic disruption causes swelling and infection risk; evidence-based lymphedema care supports drainage and function.
items.rationale: Lymphatic disruption causes swelling and infection risk; evidence-based lymphedema care supports drainage and function.

items.title: A client develops sudden severe eye pain, halos, headache, nausea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Arrange immediate ophthalmic emergency care and administer prescribed pressure-lowering therapy.
items.rationale: Acute angle-closure glaucoma threatens vision and requires immediate reduction of intraocular pressure.

items.title: A client reports sudden flashes, floaters, and a curtain-like shadow over one eye. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Arrange same-day emergency ophthalmology evaluation, limit activity as instructed, and prepare for definitive treatment.
items.rationale: A curtain-like visual field defect suggests retinal detachment; prompt repair preserves vision.

items.title: A client 1 day after cataract surgery reports mild scratchiness but no severe pain or vision loss. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Reinforce eye-drop schedule, shield use, avoiding heavy lifting/straining, and urgent reporting of severe pain or sudden vision change.
items.rationale: Mild irritation may occur; severe pain or sudden loss of vision is not expected and needs urgent review.

items.title: A client has episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating unilateral hearing loss. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client has episodic vertigo, tinnitus, and fluctuating unilateral hearing loss.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Institute fall precautions during attacks, teach low-sodium plan if prescribed, and administer ordered symptom control.
items.rationale: Vertigo creates fall risk; dietary and medication management may reduce episodes.

items.title: A client receiving a potentially ototoxic medication reports new tinnitus and hearing difficulty. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client receiving a potentially ototoxic medication reports new tinnitus and hearing difficulty.|response:Report promptly, review drug levels/renal function and alternatives, and arrange hearing assessment.|rationale:Early tinnitus may precede permanent hearing loss from ototoxic medications.
items.rationale: Early tinnitus may precede permanent hearing loss from ototoxic medications.

items.title: A toddler has ear pain, fever, and bulging tympanic membrane. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Acute otitis media|priority:Provide analgesia, assess age/severity and follow clinician plan for observation or antibiotics, and teach completion if prescribed.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Many cases are self-limited; treatment depends on age, severity, laterality, and follow-up reliability.

items.title: A client has anterior nosebleed after dry air exposure and is hemodynamically stable. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Epistaxis|actions:Sit upright, lean forward, pinch soft part of nose continuously for 10–15 minutes, and avoid tilting head back.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Forward positioning prevents swallowing blood; sustained pressure is first-line for uncomplicated anterior bleeding.

items.title: A client receiving chemotherapy has painful oral ulcers and difficulty eating. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client receiving chemotherapy has painful oral ulcers and difficulty eating.|priority:Assess hydration/nutrition, provide gentle oral care and prescribed analgesia, avoid alcohol-based rinses, and monitor infection.
items.rationale: Mucositis compromises intake and mucosal barrier; gentle care and symptom management are essential.

items.title: A client receiving external-beam radiation has mild erythema in the treatment field. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Radiated skin is fragile; gentle care reduces irritation and treatment disruption.

items.title: A vesicant chemotherapy infusion site becomes painful, swollen, and cool. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Extravasation can cause tissue necrosis; management is agent-specific and should follow protocol.

items.title: A client with cancer reports new severe back pain worse when lying down and with coughing. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Assess neurologic function and sphincter symptoms, notify oncology team urgently, and arrange urgent imaging for possible metastasis/compression.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: New progressive back pain in cancer may precede spinal cord compression.

items.title: A client with severe neutropenia has inflamed gums and oral soreness. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Use soft toothbrush or approved gentle oral-care method, avoid flossing if thrombocytopenic, and report ulcers/fever.
items.rationale: Gentle oral care reduces mucosal injury and infection risk; adapt to platelet count.

items.title: A dying client has noisy upper-airway secretions but no visible distress. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:End-of-life secretion management|actions:Reposition laterally, provide gentle mouth care, explain the sound to family, and use prescribed anticholinergic only if appropriate.|evaluation:Noisy secretions often distress observers more than the patient; avoid deep suction that causes discomfort.
items.rationale: Noisy secretions often distress observers more than the patient; avoid deep suction that causes discomfort.

items.title: A client transitioning between opioid formulations has a new dose calculated from an equianalgesic table. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Verify conversion with prescriber/pharmacist, apply incomplete cross-tolerance reduction when appropriate, and monitor sedation/respiration.
items.rationale: Equianalgesic conversions are estimates; incomplete cross-tolerance and patient factors affect safe dosing.

items.title: A client with advanced disease asks whether choosing hospice means all care stops. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Explain hospice focuses on comfort and goals, continues symptom treatment and support, and review eligibility/services with hospice team.
items.rationale: Hospice changes the care focus, not the commitment to active symptom management and support.

items.title: A 62-year-old reports crushing substernal pressure radiating to the jaw for 25 minutes; skin is cool and ECG shows ST elevation in contiguous leads. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Activate emergency response, obtain/interpret 12-lead ECG, establish IV access, give aspirin if not contraindicated, and prepare for reperfusion.
items.rationale: Time-dependent myocardial injury requires rapid recognition and reperfusion; assess contraindications and follow ACS protocol.

items.title: A 71-year-old develops facial droop and unilateral arm weakness 40 minutes ago; bedside glucose is 108 mg/dL. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A 71-year-old develops facial droop and unilateral arm weakness 40 minutes ago; bedside glucose is 108 mg/dL.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Activate stroke pathway, establish last-known-well time, check glucose, obtain urgent noncontrast head CT, and keep NPO pending swallow screen.
items.rationale: Rapid imaging distinguishes hemorrhage from ischemia; last-known-well guides reperfusion eligibility and swallowing precautions reduce aspiration.

items.title: A client with pneumonia is febrile, confused, BP 82/46 mm Hg, HR 128/min, lactate 4.2 mmol/L. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client with pneumonia is febrile, confused, BP 82/46 mm Hg, HR 128/min, lactate 4.2 mmol/L.|response:Escalate immediately, obtain cultures without delaying antibiotics, administer prescribed broad-spectrum antimicrobials and crystalloid, and reassess perfusion.|rationale:Hypotension and elevated lactate suggest septic shock; timely antimicrobials, fluid resuscitation, and reassessment are essential.
items.rationale: Hypotension and elevated lactate suggest septic shock; timely antimicrobials, fluid resuscitation, and reassessment are essential.

items.title: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes has vomiting, deep respirations, glucose 486 mg/dL, pH 7.18, bicarbonate 10 mEq/L, and potassium 5.4 mEq/L. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Diabetic ketoacidosis|priority:Begin isotonic IV fluids, monitor potassium and ECG, initiate IV insulin per protocol after potassium assessment, and track glucose/anion gap.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: DKA requires volume replacement and insulin; serum potassium may be elevated despite total-body depletion and can fall rapidly with treatment.

items.title: An older adult with type 2 diabetes has profound dehydration, glucose 890 mg/dL, serum osmolality 342 mOsm/kg, and minimal ketones. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state|actions:Prioritize isotonic fluid replacement, frequent neurologic and electrolyte assessment, and insulin per protocol after initial fluids.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Severe hyperosmolality and dehydration dominate HHS; gradual correction and close monitoring reduce neurologic and circulatory complications.

items.title: A client with heart failure is acutely dyspneic, has diffuse crackles, pink frothy sputum, and SpO₂ 82%. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with heart failure is acutely dyspneic, has diffuse crackles, pink frothy sputum, and SpO₂ 82%.|priority:Sit upright, support oxygenation/ventilation, summon emergency assistance, and prepare prescribed diuretic/vasodilator therapy.
items.rationale: Pulmonary edema causes acute gas-exchange failure; respiratory support and rapid escalation take priority.

items.title: A client with acute kidney injury has potassium 6.8 mEq/L and peaked T waves on ECG. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: ECG changes indicate cardiac toxicity; calcium stabilizes the myocardium while other therapies lower serum potassium.

items.title: A client receiving loop diuretics has weakness, potassium 2.7 mEq/L, and flattened T waves. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Hypokalemia increases dysrhythmia risk; IV potassium must never be given by IV push.

items.title: A postoperative client has urine output 15 mL/hr for 3 hours and creatinine rising from 0.9 to 2.1 mg/dL. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Assess volume status and perfusion, review nephrotoxic exposures, notify the provider, and trend urine output/electrolytes.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Oliguria and rising creatinine indicate impaired renal function requiring prompt evaluation of reversible causes.

items.title: A client with COPD has increased work of breathing, wheezing, and SpO₂ 86% on room air; baseline target is 88–92%. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Titrate controlled oxygen to the prescribed target, administer bronchodilators, assess for fatigue, and obtain blood gas as ordered.
items.rationale: Controlled oxygen and bronchodilation improve hypoxemia/airflow while monitoring for hypercapnia and respiratory failure.

items.title: A 19-year-old has severe wheezing, accessory muscle use, and speaks only one word at a time. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Asthma exacerbation|actions:Treat as severe exacerbation: urgent escalation, inhaled short-acting bronchodilator, systemic corticosteroid, oxygen, and reassessment.|evaluation:Inability to speak full sentences and accessory muscle use indicate severe airflow obstruction.
items.rationale: Inability to speak full sentences and accessory muscle use indicate severe airflow obstruction.

items.title: A postoperative client develops sudden pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, dyspnea, and SpO₂ 88%. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Escalate immediately, support oxygenation, assess hemodynamic stability, and prepare for diagnostic evaluation and anticoagulation if prescribed.
items.rationale: Acute dyspnea and pleuritic pain after surgery raise concern for PE; instability requires emergency response.

items.title: A chest drainage system becomes disconnected from the chest tube while the client is coughing. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Restore a sterile water seal per facility protocol, keep the system below chest level, assess respiratory status, and notify the provider.
items.rationale: Maintaining a water seal limits air entry; never clamp a chest tube routinely because tension pneumothorax may result.

items.title: A client after central-line insertion develops severe dyspnea, hypotension, absent breath sounds on one side, and tracheal deviation. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Call emergency response and prepare for immediate decompression; provide oxygen and support circulation.
items.rationale: Obstructive shock with unilateral absent breath sounds is a life-threatening tension pneumothorax.

items.title: A client reports hematemesis and melena; BP is 86/52 mm Hg and HR 132/min. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A client reports hematemesis and melena; BP is 86/52 mm Hg and HR 132/min.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Assess airway and perfusion, activate urgent response, establish large-bore IV access, prepare fluids/blood products, and trend CBC/coagulation.
items.rationale: Hemodynamic instability suggests significant hemorrhage; circulation and airway protection are priorities.

items.title: A client has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase four times the upper reference limit, and persistent vomiting. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client has severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, lipase four times the upper reference limit, and persistent vomiting.|response:Provide prescribed IV fluids and analgesia, monitor respiratory/renal status and electrolytes, and advance nutrition as clinically tolerated.|rationale:Pancreatitis care emphasizes supportive treatment, hydration, pain control, and surveillance for organ dysfunction.
items.rationale: Pancreatitis care emphasizes supportive treatment, hydration, pain control, and surveillance for organ dysfunction.

items.title: A client has abdominal distention, colicky pain, bilious vomiting, and absent stool/flatus. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Bowel obstruction|priority:Keep NPO, initiate prescribed IV fluids, monitor electrolytes and abdominal findings, and prepare for imaging/decompression.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Obstruction risks fluid shifts, ischemia, and perforation; avoid oral intake until evaluated.

items.title: A client with suspected perforated viscus has rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness, fever, and tachycardia. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Peritonitis|actions:Escalate urgently, keep NPO, obtain IV access, prepare broad-spectrum antibiotics and surgical evaluation.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Peritoneal signs may indicate perforation and sepsis requiring urgent source control.

items.title: A client with cirrhosis is newly confused with asterixis and elevated ammonia. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client with cirrhosis is newly confused with asterixis and elevated ammonia.|priority:Assess airway and neurologic status, identify precipitating factors such as bleeding/infection/constipation, and administer prescribed lactulose.
items.rationale: Hepatic encephalopathy requires treatment of precipitants and reduction of intestinal ammonia.

items.title: A client with atrial fibrillation reports sudden severe leg pain; the foot is pale, cool, and pulseless. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: The six Ps indicate acute arterial occlusion; rapid intervention preserves limb viability.

items.title: A client with a tibial fracture reports escalating pain despite opioids and pain with passive toe stretch. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch are early signs; palpable pulses do not exclude compartment syndrome.

items.title: After trauma, a client has hypotension, bradycardia, warm dry skin, and motor weakness below the injury. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Maintain spinal alignment, support airway/breathing, monitor perfusion, and escalate for neurogenic shock management.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Loss of sympathetic tone can cause hypotension and bradycardia; spinal precautions prevent secondary injury.

items.title: A client with traumatic brain injury develops decreasing level of consciousness, vomiting, and unequal pupils. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Escalate immediately, maintain airway and neutral head alignment, elevate head about 30 degrees if not contraindicated, and avoid hip flexion.
items.rationale: Neurologic deterioration and pupillary change suggest rising ICP and possible herniation.

items.title: A hospitalized client begins generalized tonic-clonic movements while in bed. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Seizure|actions:Protect from injury, lower bed, turn to side when possible, time seizure, do not restrain or place objects in mouth, and assess airway afterward.|evaluation:Safety and airway protection are priorities; nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure.
items.rationale: Safety and airway protection are priorities; nothing should be placed in the mouth during a seizure.

items.title: A client has fever, severe headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, and altered mental status. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Initiate droplet precautions promptly, notify provider, obtain cultures/diagnostics as ordered, and do not delay prescribed antibiotics.
items.rationale: Suspected bacterial meningitis is time critical and requires isolation and prompt antimicrobial therapy.

items.title: A client receiving chemotherapy has temperature 38.4°C and absolute neutrophil count 300 cells/mm³. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Treat as an emergency: notify provider, obtain cultures, initiate prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly, and avoid rectal procedures.
items.rationale: Fever with severe neutropenia can rapidly progress to sepsis; avoid mucosal trauma and delays.

items.title: Fifteen minutes after packed RBCs begin, a client develops chills, back pain, and fever. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Stop transfusion, keep IV open with normal saline using new tubing, assess vitals, notify provider and blood bank, and follow reaction protocol.
items.rationale: Stopping the transfusion prevents further exposure; do not restart the same unit.

items.title: Minutes after an antibiotic, a client develops wheezing, facial swelling, urticaria, and BP 78/40 mm Hg. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:Minutes after an antibiotic, a client develops wheezing, facial swelling, urticaria, and BP 78/40 mm Hg.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Give IM epinephrine promptly per emergency protocol, call for help, support airway/oxygenation, and prepare IV fluids.
items.rationale: Epinephrine is first-line for anaphylaxis with airway or circulatory compromise.

items.title: A postoperative client is difficult to arouse, RR 6/min, and pupils are pinpoint after IV morphine. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A postoperative client is difficult to arouse, RR 6/min, and pupils are pinpoint after IV morphine.|response:Support ventilation, stimulate and call for help, administer naloxone per protocol, and monitor for recurrent respiratory depression.|rationale:Respiratory depression is the immediate threat; naloxone may wear off before the opioid.
items.rationale: Respiratory depression is the immediate threat; naloxone may wear off before the opioid.

items.title: A client 18 hours after last alcohol use has tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and visual hallucinations. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Alcohol withdrawal|priority:Initiate withdrawal assessment protocol, institute seizure/fall precautions, administer prescribed benzodiazepine, and give thiamine as ordered.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Withdrawal can progress to seizures or delirium tremens; benzodiazepines are first-line and thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy.

items.title: A client taking warfarin reports black stools and dizziness; INR is 5.8 and BP is 94/60 mm Hg. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Warfarin-associated bleeding|actions:Hold warfarin, assess hemodynamics, notify provider urgently, obtain CBC/type and screen, and prepare reversal therapy as prescribed.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Melena with supratherapeutic INR indicates potentially serious bleeding requiring stabilization and reversal assessment.

items.title: A client receiving unfractionated heparin has platelets fall from 220,000 to 88,000/mm³ on day 6. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A client receiving unfractionated heparin has platelets fall from 220,000 to 88,000/mm³ on day 6.|priority:Stop all heparin products, notify provider, avoid platelet transfusion unless specifically indicated, and anticipate a non-heparin anticoagulant.
items.rationale: A greater than 50% platelet fall in the typical time window suggests HIT, a prothrombotic immune reaction.

items.title: An older adult taking digoxin reports nausea and yellow vision; pulse is 48/min and potassium is 3.0 mEq/L. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Bradycardia, visual changes, and hypokalemia increase concern for digoxin toxicity.

items.title: A client with type 1 diabetes is prescribed rapid-acting insulin before meals; the meal tray is delayed. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin can cause hypoglycemia if food is delayed or unavailable.

items.title: A client receiving magnesium sulfate has RR 10/min, absent patellar reflexes, and urine output 20 mL/hr. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Stop magnesium infusion, notify provider, support breathing, and prepare prescribed calcium gluconate.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Respiratory depression and absent reflexes indicate magnesium toxicity; calcium gluconate is the antidote.

items.title: A client taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse tremor, ataxia, and confusion after several days of diarrhea. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Hold lithium, obtain serum lithium and renal/electrolyte studies, notify provider, and assess hydration and neurologic status.
items.rationale: Dehydration and sodium loss reduce lithium clearance and can precipitate toxicity.

items.title: During rapid vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and itching of face and upper torso without airway compromise. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Vancomycin infusion reaction|actions:Pause infusion, assess airway and vital signs, notify provider, and restart more slowly if prescribed after symptoms resolve.|evaluation:Rate-related histamine release can cause flushing; distinguish it from anaphylaxis and follow prescribed rate adjustments.
items.rationale: Rate-related histamine release can cause flushing; distinguish it from anaphylaxis and follow prescribed rate adjustments.

items.title: A client taking lisinopril develops tongue swelling and hoarseness. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Stop the medication, activate emergency airway response, and prepare for airway management.
items.rationale: ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema can rapidly obstruct the airway; airway protection takes priority.

items.title: A client taking metformin is scheduled for iodinated contrast and has eGFR 28 mL/min/1.73 m². During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Notify the prescriber/radiology team and follow protocol to withhold metformin around contrast and reassess renal function before restarting.
items.rationale: Renal impairment increases risk of metformin accumulation and lactic acidosis; follow current contrast and renal guidance.

items.title: A family member asks to press the client's PCA button while the client sleeps. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Explain that only the client should activate PCA, assess sedation and respiratory status, and reinforce safety.
items.rationale: PCA by proxy increases risk of oversedation because the client cannot self-limit doses.

items.title: A nurse prepares IV potassium chloride for a client with potassium 2.8 mEq/L. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A nurse prepares IV potassium chloride for a client with potassium 2.8 mEq/L.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Dilute and administer via infusion pump at prescribed rate after checking renal function and urine output; never give IV push.
items.rationale: Concentrated potassium can cause fatal dysrhythmias if administered rapidly.

items.title: A client taking long-term prednisone reports fever and has fasting glucose 220 mg/dL. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A client taking long-term prednisone reports fever and has fasting glucose 220 mg/dL.|response:Assess for infection and hyperglycemia, teach not to stop abruptly, and discuss lowest effective dose/taper only as prescribed.|rationale:Corticosteroids suppress immune response, raise glucose, and require tapering after prolonged use.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress immune response, raise glucose, and require tapering after prolonged use.

items.title: A client receiving gentamicin reports tinnitus and has rising creatinine. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Aminoglycoside toxicity|priority:Hold dose pending urgent review, notify provider, and assess renal function and drug levels as ordered.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Aminoglycosides can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity; early symptoms warrant prompt evaluation.

items.title: A client receiving phenytoin has nystagmus, ataxia, and slurred speech. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Phenytoin toxicity|actions:Institute fall precautions, obtain level and medication review, and notify provider before further dosing.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Nystagmus and ataxia are common signs of elevated phenytoin levels.

items.title: Before metoprolol, a client's HR is 48/min and BP is 90/54 mm Hg. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:Before metoprolol, a client's HR is 48/min and BP is 90/54 mm Hg.|priority:Hold dose according to prescribed parameters, assess symptoms and perfusion, and notify provider.
items.rationale: Beta blockers reduce heart rate and blood pressure; symptomatic bradycardia/hypotension requires review.

items.title: A client taking clopidogrel reports new black stools and weakness. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Clopidogrel increases bleeding risk; suspected GI hemorrhage needs urgent assessment.

items.title: An older adult is admitted with multiple medication bottles and cannot recall doses. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Multiple sources reduce omissions, duplication, and dosing errors during transitions.

items.title: Twenty minutes after birth, a client has heavy vaginal bleeding and a boggy fundus. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Call for assistance, massage the fundus, assess bladder and vital signs, quantify blood loss, and prepare uterotonics/resuscitation.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Uterine atony is a common cause of postpartum hemorrhage; rapid response limits shock.

items.title: A 34-week pregnant client has BP 168/112 mm Hg, severe headache, and visual spots. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Escalate urgently, institute seizure precautions, administer prescribed antihypertensive and magnesium sulfate, and monitor reflexes/respiration.
items.rationale: Severe-range hypertension and neurologic symptoms increase risk of stroke and eclampsia.

items.title: A pregnant client with preeclampsia begins a tonic-clonic seizure. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Eclampsia|actions:Protect airway and client from injury, position laterally when possible, call emergency response, and administer magnesium sulfate per protocol.|evaluation:Maternal stabilization and seizure control are immediate priorities; avoid restraining the client.
items.rationale: Maternal stabilization and seizure control are immediate priorities; avoid restraining the client.

items.title: A 32-week pregnant client has painless bright-red vaginal bleeding and a soft nontender uterus. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Avoid vaginal examination, assess maternal/fetal status, establish IV access, and notify obstetric team.
items.rationale: Digital examination can disrupt placenta previa and cause catastrophic hemorrhage.

items.title: A pregnant client has sudden abdominal pain, dark bleeding, uterine tenderness, and frequent contractions. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Escalate immediately, assess maternal circulation and fetal status, establish IV access, and prepare for urgent delivery if indicated.
items.rationale: Painful bleeding and uterine tenderness suggest abruption with risk of maternal hemorrhage and fetal compromise.

items.title: After membrane rupture, fetal heart rate falls to 70/min and the cord is visible at the introitus. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Call emergency obstetric response, use a gloved hand to lift presenting part off cord, position knee-chest/Trendelenburg, and prepare for immediate birth.
items.rationale: Relieving cord compression preserves fetal oxygenation while expediting delivery.

items.title: During oxytocin infusion, recurrent late decelerations occur with contractions. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:During oxytocin infusion, recurrent late decelerations occur with contractions.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Stop oxytocin, reposition laterally, increase IV fluids as appropriate, assess maternal BP, and notify obstetric provider.
items.rationale: Late decelerations suggest uteroplacental insufficiency; reduce uterine stimulation and improve perfusion.

items.title: After delivery of the fetal head, the shoulders fail to deliver and the turtle sign appears. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:After delivery of the fetal head, the shoulders fail to deliver and the turtle sign appears.|response:Call for help and assist with McRoberts maneuver and suprapubic pressure; never apply fundal pressure.|rationale:Shoulder dystocia requires maneuvers that widen pelvic outlet and release impacted shoulder; fundal pressure worsens impaction.
items.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires maneuvers that widen pelvic outlet and release impacted shoulder; fundal pressure worsens impaction.

items.title: An infant of a diabetic mother is jittery at 1 hour of life; bedside glucose is 32 mg/dL. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Newborn hypoglycemia|priority:Follow neonatal hypoglycemia protocol: feed promptly if stable and able, recheck glucose, and give dextrose gel/IV glucose as indicated.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Jitteriness may signal hypoglycemia; prompt treatment prevents neurologic injury.

items.title: A term newborn has grunting, nasal flaring, retractions, and central cyanosis. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Newborn respiratory distress|actions:Call neonatal team, maintain warmth, support airway/oxygenation, and monitor preductal saturation.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Grunting and retractions indicate respiratory distress requiring prompt stabilization.

items.title: Two days after cesarean birth, a client has fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:Two days after cesarean birth, a client has fever, uterine tenderness, and foul-smelling lochia.|priority:Notify provider, obtain ordered cultures, administer prescribed broad-spectrum antibiotics, and monitor for sepsis.
items.rationale: Postpartum fever with uterine tenderness and malodorous lochia suggests uterine infection.

items.title: An unsensitized Rh-negative client delivers an Rh-positive infant. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Rh immune globulin prevents maternal sensitization and future hemolytic disease.

items.title: A client at 30 weeks has regular contractions and cervical change. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Place the nursing actions in the safest priority sequence.
items.content: sequence:Recognize deterioration and assess ABCs|Escalate and obtain assistance|Implement prescribed immediate intervention|Reassess response and document
items.rationale: Corticosteroids improve fetal lung maturity; tocolysis may allow time for treatment when safe.

items.title: A breastfeeding client has unilateral breast erythema, fever, and flu-like symptoms. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select all findings and interventions that belong in the immediate plan of care.
items.content: answer:Encourage continued milk removal, assess latch and abscess signs, provide comfort measures, and administer prescribed antibiotics when bacterial mastitis is suspected.|include:Focused reassessment; safety precautions; timely escalation; evaluation of response
items.rationale: Milk removal supports recovery; untreated bacterial infection may progress to abscess.

items.title: A 4-year-old has high fever, drooling, tripod posture, and muffled voice. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Compare the current findings with the earlier baseline and identify deterioration and the next action.
items.content: trend:Current findings indicate possible deterioration|action:Keep child calm and upright, avoid throat inspection or tongue depressor, and summon airway-capable emergency team.
items.rationale: Manipulating the airway can precipitate complete obstruction in suspected epiglottitis.

items.title: A 2-year-old has barking cough, inspiratory stridor at rest, and suprasternal retractions. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. Use the clinical cues to prioritize hypotheses, actions, and reassessment.
items.content: priority:Croup|actions:Keep child calm, provide prescribed corticosteroid and nebulized epinephrine for moderate/severe symptoms, and monitor after treatment.|evaluation:Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway narrowing; nebulized epinephrine has temporary effect and requires observation.
items.rationale: Stridor at rest indicates significant upper-airway narrowing; nebulized epinephrine has temporary effect and requires observation.

items.title: An 8-month-old with RSV has nasal congestion, poor feeding, RR 62/min, and mild retractions. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Select the single best immediate nursing action.
items.content: answer:Assess work of breathing and hydration, suction nasal secretions, provide oxygen if indicated, and support hydration.
items.rationale: Bronchiolitis treatment is primarily supportive; nasal suction can improve feeding and breathing.

items.title: A toddler has vomiting and diarrhea, dry mucosa, sunken eyes, and capillary refill 4 seconds. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Select all actions that are appropriate for the findings.
items.content: answer:Assess severity and perfusion, begin oral rehydration if mild/moderate and able, or isotonic IV bolus for shock/severe dehydration per protocol.
items.rationale: Rehydration route depends on perfusion and ability to tolerate oral fluids.

items.title: A child has 6 days of fever, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctivitis, strawberry tongue, rash, and swollen hands. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Select the four priority actions supported by the clinical findings.
items.content: answer:Notify provider promptly and anticipate IV immunoglobulin and aspirin therapy with cardiac evaluation.
items.rationale: Early treatment reduces risk of coronary artery aneurysm.

items.title: A 10-month-old has episodic severe crying, draws knees to chest, vomits, and passes currant-jelly stool. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Classify each finding as expected, concerning, or requiring immediate escalation.
items.content: finding:A 10-month-old has episodic severe crying, draws knees to chest, vomits, and passes currant-jelly stool.|classification:Requires focused clinical assessment|key:Keep NPO, establish IV access, monitor perfusion, and prepare for ultrasound and air/contrast enema reduction.
items.rationale: Intermittent pain and bloody mucus stool suggest intussusception; enema may be diagnostic and therapeutic.

items.title: A 5-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, hunger after emesis, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis. The client is admitted to an acute-care unit; allergies and current medications are being verified. For each assessment cue, identify the matching nursing response and the reason.
items.content: cue:A 5-week-old has projectile nonbilious vomiting, hunger after emesis, and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis.|response:Correct fluid and electrolyte deficits before surgical pyloromyotomy; monitor weight and urine output.|rationale:Persistent gastric losses cause dehydration and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; stabilize before surgery.
items.rationale: Persistent gastric losses cause dehydration and hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis; stabilize before surgery.

items.title: An infant with tetralogy of Fallot becomes cyanotic and irritable during feeding. During reassessment, the nurse notes the findings have persisted despite initial comfort measures. Complete the clinical statement by selecting the priority condition, action, and monitoring parameter.
items.content: condition:Tetralogy of Fallot spell|priority:Place infant in knee-chest position, provide oxygen, calm infant, and summon provider/emergency assistance.|monitoring:Reassess vital signs, clinical response, and relevant laboratory/diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Knee-chest positioning increases systemic vascular resistance and can reduce right-to-left shunting.

items.title: A child with sickle cell disease has fever, chest pain, cough, and new pulmonary infiltrate. The client has a relevant chronic condition; compare the current assessment with the documented baseline. Identify the most likely condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:Sickle cell acute chest syndrome|actions:Escalate urgently, provide oxygen if hypoxemic, initiate prescribed antibiotics/analgesia, encourage incentive spirometry, and prepare transfusion evaluation.|monitor:Vital signs, oxygenation/perfusion, and condition-specific laboratory or diagnostic trends
items.rationale: Acute chest syndrome is life-threatening and requires prompt supportive and disease-specific care.

items.title: A 20-month-old has a generalized seizure lasting 2 minutes during fever and is now drowsy but breathing. The family asks what the nurse should do first while the provider is being contacted. Identify the assessment cues in the scenario that require immediate follow-up.
items.content: highlight:A 20-month-old has a generalized seizure lasting 2 minutes during fever and is now drowsy but breathing.|priority:Protect airway and safety, time the event, assess recovery and glucose as indicated, and educate caregiver after evaluation.
items.rationale: Brief generalized febrile seizures are often self-limited; airway safety and assessment for cause are essential.

items.title: A child has fever, lethargy, hypotension, and a rapidly spreading nonblanching petechial rash. The nurse is preparing a handoff and must identify the most time-sensitive concern. Enter the clinically relevant threshold or measurement specified in the care protocol; verify against the client context.
items.content: answer:Use the client-specific value and protocol threshold stated in the scenario; this item requires a validated numeric key before exam use.
items.rationale: Meningococcal sepsis can progress rapidly; isolation and immediate treatment are critical.
